thread.title: A Tech Option Income CEF Puzzler - Nuveen Nasdaq 100 Dynamic Overwrite Fund (NASDAQ:QQQX)

author: Stanford Chemist
title: A Tech Option Income CEF Puzzler - Nuveen Nasdaq 100 Dynamic Overwrite Fund (NASDAQ:QQQX)
text:
Buying a closed-end fund [CEF] at a high premium is a mistake on several levels, in my opinion. Firstly, it opens up the possibility of devastating effects on share price if the distribution is cut (see Why CEF Distribution Stability Is Overvalued ). Secondly, having a high premium can incentivize management to conduct rights offerings, which also has a deleterious effect on share price (see Gabelli Utility Trust's Rights Offering Oversubscribed for a recent example). Third, each time a CEF at a significant premium makes a distribution, alpha is lost .
Now, some investors may ask: who cares about a premium, as long as my income stream remains steady? I'll be the first to say that a purely income-focused, buy-and-hold approach is a perfectly valid way of investing, and it's very easy to execute as well to boot. However, I believe we can do better by avoiding overvalued funds , and investing in undervalued funds instead; basically a "buy low sell high" approach for CEFs. In doing so, we can potentially grow our income stream much faster than with a purely buy-and-hold approach alone (see CEF Rotation = Compounding Income On Steroids ). After all, that's why we're on "Seeking Alpha", right?
What constitutes a "high" premium is very much fund dependent, and depends on factors such as management quality, availability of alternatives, etc. For example, I give the PIMCO taxable CEFs a wide tolerance for valuation before considering to sell (see the Income Generator Portfolio for premium/discount targets) due to their expertise in the fixed income arena, strong track record and the lack of similar funds to rotate into. In fact, we're still holding onto half a position of the PIMCO Corporate & Income Strategy Fund ( PCN ) despite it exceeding our sell above premium target of 15% some weeks ago.
Conversely, a fund that simply owns a well-known index such as the NASDAQ-100 with a covered call overlay should not deserve an exceptional premium, which is why the +16.57% premium of Nuveen Nasdaq 100 Dynamic Overwrite Fund ( QQQX ) is so puzzling.
The overvaluation of QQQX is a drum that I've banged on several times in the past, as has another Seeking Alpha contributor, Douglas Albo, multiple times as well. While I accept that to be early is to be wrong, I simply cannot see any reason that a fund like QQQX should sustain such a high premium over the long term. And we should not forget that even in cases where we were early with our calls (e.g. PIMCO Global StocksPLUS & Income Fund ( PGP ) or Gabelli Utility Trust ( GUT )), we were proved right in the end as the premium did eventually collapse for one reason or another.
QQQX closed yesterday with a yield of 6.00% (paid quarterly), a premium of +16.57%, and 1-year z-score of +2.7.
Instead of QQQX, why not consider another tech option income CEF such as the Columbia Seligman Premium Technology Growth Fund ( STK )? While it's not exactly cheap at a +2.94% premium, its 1-year z-score of -0.7 indicates that it is slightly less pricey than its historical average. It yields 8.12% (paid quarterly) as well, so you're getting an extra 2 percentage points of yield with STK compared to QQQX to boot.
Here's the historical premium/discount averages for QQQX (current premium +16.57%):
1 year: +5.29% 3 year: -1.21% 5 year: -1.61% STK (current premium +2.94%):
1 year: +4.46% 3 year: +3.71% 5 year: +1.50% The numbers above clearly show that QQQX is trading far above its historical valuations, whereas STK is not.
Here's the 5-year premium/discount chart for QQQX:
STK:
Performance wise, STK significantly outperforms QQQX over 3 and 5-year time frames on a NAV basis, while being comparable over 1 year. Impressively, STK has nearly matched the benchmark's ( QQQ ) returns over 3 and 5 years despite using an option strategy, which generally underperforms during bull markets.
In fact, on a price total return basis, STK actually comes out on top over 5 years, outperforming both QQQX and QQQ.
QQQX Total Return Price data by YCharts
On the topic of benchmarks, STK is definitely not a closet indexer. The top holdings of STK shown below are very different from the top holdings of the NASDAQ.
Here's the top holdings for QQQX. We can see that only Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) are common top holdings between the two funds.
STK charges 1.15% in baseline expense ratio, versus 0.94% for QQQX, so STK is about 20 bps more expensive by that measure. However, it may be worth it considering the high active share of STK that has historically produced fruit versus the benchmark.
It should also be noted that STK has more flexibility on the call option coverage overlaid on the fund, at 25% to 90% (nominal average 57.5%). In contrast, QQQX aims to cover between 35% to 75% of the portfolio, with a 55% long term target.
Summary If I were a holder of QQQX I'd be counting my lucky stars at being able to achieve a price return that was significantly higher than both the benchmark QQQ, and the peer fund STK.
QQQX Total Return Price data by YCharts
However, this outperformance has been entirely due to QQQX's exploding premium.
QQQX Discount or Premium to NAV data by YCharts
Therefore, selling QQQX to lock in paper profits and rotating into STK offers good odds for outperformance from premium/discount reversion.
For the more adventurous, iBorrowDesk shows 600 shares of QQQX available to short at a very expensive fee rate of 17.2%. The fee rate spiked up at around the same time as the premium of QQQX ramped up, which is probably not a coincidence.
July 7, 2018 update
Since the idea was released to our members around 3 weeks ago, STK has outperformed QQQX by over 200 bps (>35% annualized).
QQQX Total Return Price data by YCharts
While the premia of both QQQX and STK fell, QQQX's fell more (by over 6%), causing the relative valuation difference to move in our favor.
QQQX Discount or Premium to NAV data by YCharts
Currently STK trades with a premium of +0.79% and a 1-year z-score of -1.6, whereas QQQX trades with a premium of +10.16% and a z-score of +0.8, so this trade may still have room to run further.
